title: Sell Mineral Rights in Louisiana
group: Haynesville, Tuscaloosa Marine Shale, Gulf Coast
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Louisiana | Haynesville+
metaDescription: Active Haynesville gas well, quiet Tuscaloosa Marine Shale acreage, or legacy Gulf Coast oil interest? Three different Louisiana plays, three different offers.
heroLead: Where your Louisiana acreage sits inside the play matters as much as which play it's in, core Haynesville acreage behaves nothing like its flank, and neither behaves like Gulf Coast legacy production.
intro: Louisiana carries three distinct royalty stories depending on where your interest sits. The Haynesville shale, running through Caddo, Bossier, and DeSoto parishes, is genuinely active today, driven largely by LNG export demand for natural gas, and operators are still permitting and drilling new wells in the core of the play. If your check is Haynesville, you may be looking at one of the few gas plays in the country with real near-term drilling activity behind it.

South of there, the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale, spanning parishes near the Louisiana-Mississippi line, told a different story. Early operators drilled a wave of wells starting around 2013, ran into difficult geology and high costs, and mostly pulled back within a few years. Most TMS acreage today sits quiet, with owners holding leases or small legacy production rather than active drilling. And along the coast, Gulf Coast parishes like Cameron and Vermilion carry a much older history of conventional oil and gas, much of it declining steadily for decades.

sections.heading: Core Haynesville vs. the Flank
paragraphs: Not all Haynesville acreage is equal. Core counties, Caddo, Bossier, DeSoto, sit over the thickest, most productive part of the shale and continue to see active drilling. Flank acreage on the edges of the play has historically drawn less operator interest and thinner results, even within the same general region.

That distinction matters directly for an offer. Core Haynesville production with recent drilling nearby is priced very differently than flank acreage with an older, quieter well and no permits filed nearby, and we tell owners plainly which situation they are in before any number comes up.

sections.heading: Tuscaloosa Marine Shale: A Boom That Mostly Didn't Happen
paragraphs: If you hold TMS acreage, the honest history is that the play underperformed the early hype. High well costs and inconsistent results led most operators to scale back drilling within a few years of the initial rush, and large-scale development that was once expected simply has not materialized since.

That does not make a TMS interest worthless, but it does mean valuing it requires an honest look at whatever production history actually exists rather than pricing off the optimism that surrounded the play a decade ago.

sections.heading: Gulf Coast Legacy Production Reads Like an Old Field
paragraphs: Cameron, Vermilion, and other Gulf Coast parishes carry decades of conventional oil and gas history, much of it mature fields in steady, well-understood decline. These checks tend to be smaller and more predictable than a shale check, closer in character to legacy production you would find in Texas's older fields.

Owners here are often multiple generations removed from whoever signed the original lease, and interests can be fractional across several heirs, which is worth accounting for before assuming your offer will reflect a full undivided interest.

sections.heading: Getting an Offer Built for Your Specific Play
paragraphs: Send us your most recent statement and, if you have it, the well or unit name. That tells us immediately whether you are in core or flank Haynesville, TMS, or a Gulf Coast legacy field, and each of those gets evaluated on its own recent production history and, where relevant, nearby permitted activity.

Closing runs through a mineral deed and a title check at the parish clerk of court where the interest is recorded, and timelines are typically a few weeks once ownership and any heirship questions are sorted out.

faqs.question: Is the Haynesville shale still being actively drilled?
faqs.answer: Yes, particularly in the core counties of Caddo, Bossier, and DeSoto parish, where LNG export demand has kept drilling activity going in recent years, more than in most other gas plays nationally.

faqs.question: What happened to the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale?
faqs.answer: Early operators drilled aggressively starting around 2013 but ran into difficult geology and high costs, and most scaled back development within a few years. Large-scale drilling in the play has not resumed since.

faqs.question: Why is your Gulf Coast Louisiana check so much smaller than a Haynesville check?
faqs.answer: Gulf Coast parishes carry much older, more mature conventional production that has been declining for decades, so checks there tend to be smaller and steadier than newer shale gas production further north.

faqs.question: How do you know if your acreage is core or flank Haynesville?
faqs.answer: The parish and section-township-range on your statement or lease, along with nearby permitted well activity, tell us where your acreage sits within the play. We check this before discussing any offer.

faqs.question: Does LNG export demand actually affect what your Haynesville royalty is worth?
faqs.answer: It has been a real driver of continued drilling interest in the play, since export terminals along the Gulf Coast create demand for the gas Haynesville wells produce. That said, offers are still built from your specific well's documented production, not broader market narratives.

faqs.question: Your Louisiana interest is held through a succession that was never completed. Can you still sell?
faqs.answer: It is workable, but a Louisiana succession, the state's version of probate, needs to be resolved or at least underway before a clean transfer can close. We can walk you through what that typically involves for a mineral interest specifically.
